newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russia's boy soldiers learn hard facts of life.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russia's boy soldiers learn hard facts of life.

text.p: Kolya is a happy, healthy nine-year-old who has a dream many older Russian boys would consider very odd indeed.

Kolya wants to be an army officer, eager to join the ranks of those who would rather dodge their conscription to avoid two years in Russia's cash-strapped and run-down forces, where officers go without pay for months and hungry soldiers beg in the streets.

"I like it, it's fun," said Kolya, who just spent four weeks of tough-as-nails training at a children's military camp in the forest near the village of Boyarkino, some 150 km (90 miles) south of Moscow.

He and about 20 other Russian boys have been put through an ambitious drill programme, including marching, ambush training, exercises and hygiene lessons, which the organisers say may be hard but could save the youngsters' lives one day.
Kolya, wearing baggy, worn-out battle fatigues and running shoes, is the baby of the unit. But he has already learned that life in Russia's armed forces can be very tough.
MOCK BATTLES END IN TEARS

"Soldier! Where are your ears?" howled Gennady Korotayev, a former officer in the interior ministry troops whose gruff attitude hides a warm heart. "Those are mines!" he yelled at Kolya. "And you, you walked right over them."
The boy, exhausted after an hour of running and crawling over an open field, had forgotten for a moment that the tiny clumps of smouldering straw scattered around him were make-believe landmines.
Kolya caught his breath, grabbed his gun, a dummy Kalashinikov of regulation weight, pushed the oversized helmet over his face and rubbed his eyes with dirty fingers.
No one was meant to see his tears.
The instructors, all of them former or active officers, insist, however, that few tears flow in the camp.
"There was one boy who was homesick. He cried every morning. But after three days, he stopped. He didn't want to leave any more," Mikhail Muravyov, one of the camp organisers.
For years, Muravyov, Korotayev and others have spent their entire annual holidays training young boys from nine to 17, who all come to the camps of their own free will.
According to Russian estimates there are some 10 military children camps in the Moscow region, giving boys an idea of what life in Russia's vast conscript army will be like.
In Boyarkino they sleep in army tents, follow a military timetable, which also includes washing their little white uniform collar-bands every night.
INSTRUCTORS SAY BOYS HAVE TO SURVIVE IN TOUGH ARMY
Some boys are regular visitors, like Artur, a 17-year-old medical student who, unlike young Kolya, harbours no romantic ideas about the army but just wants to be well prepared for it.
"If you've been here, you know more or less what to expect. You're not that frightened of doing your service any more," he said.
Boys like Artur and his camp comrades have little chance of escaping the call-up, which is compulsory -- at least in theory.
Rich and well-connected parents often buy their sons out, handing over huge bribes to army officers or exploiting their high-level contacts.
"We don't get the sons of bosses or parents with such money," said Korotayev. These boys here have to go -- and they have to cope."

His main desire is to help them survive in often cruel army units, where officers and older soldiers often bully young conscripts, driving some to desert or even kill themselves. Some bullied youngsters have snapped and murdered their tormentors.

President Boris Yeltsin says he is eager to reform and modernise the army, plagued by theft, high-level corruption and crime. He is well aware that his nation's youth consider military service a very unattractive prospect.

Fighting for re-election last year, he even promised to scrap conscription altogether by the year 2000. That deadline seems since to have been quietly dropped, however, as a professional army is beyond Russia's budget at the moment.

Failing the end of conscription, the president has tried to make youngsters see it in a better light. "You should not get scared of the men in uniform, you should rather envy them," he told a group of Moscow high school graduates in May.
THOUSANDS DESERT

But hundreds, maybe thousands, disagree and vote with their feet. More than 230 men deserted within one week in July, a defence ministry source said last month. Officially, some 4,000 soldiers have fled the service since 1992. The real figure may be much higher.
Korotayev too is upset by the poor state of the armed forces: "The situation cannot be described in proper words."
Apart from poor conditions and bullying, the lack of proper training was blamed for heavy casualties among conscripts during Moscow's disastrous Afghan and Chechen campaigns.
The summer camps, therefore, try to make up for it.
"All the boys who stayed with us and had to go and fight in Afghanistan and later Chechnya made it back home. Some were wounded. But none was killed," Korotayev said.

Only some of the boy soldiers go on to take up professional soldiering or police work. Some turn their training to other ends. "A couple of them have gone into bandit gangs," Korotayev said. "And they help us out financially, from time to time."
